title: Chapter 97 – Fragment of a Name
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

By the sixth week the cold has settled into the mountain like a tenant who intends to stay.

The pool in front of the long hall is frozen to the bottom. The orange fish are gone from under the ice, or sleeping so deep that they might as well be. Icicles hang from the eaves of the bell tower as long as a man's arm, and each morning the Iron Bone drill is held on a lawn of blue glass, with Kuang's pole ringing off frozen shoulders like a hammer on an anvil. Jian has stopped feeling the strikes. He has begun to feel something else instead, in the marrow, a quiet that was not there before.

His body has moved. Step four has become step five. The Mirror has not been asked, and he has not volunteered. But Kuang stood over him on the thirty-fourth morning with her pole raised, and let it fall, and did not speak, and he knew by the set of her mouth that his bones had caught up.

Qi step five. Body step five. Soul four. The spread is a single step again. It is the frame the Dock told him he needed.

What has not moved is the Spring Vein. It lies in his left arm like a cut cord, gray under the skin, and no breath of his can warm it. Every morning he lays a palm on the frozen lawn and tries to draw, and every morning the vein answers with a faint dull ache and nothing else. The living source it feeds on has died back with the year. It will not wake until the thaw.

Until then I am what I am, he thinks. A man with a base, a Seal, and a handful of tricks that cost more than they give.

It is a poor inventory. It will have to do. Even so, the Sect's ledgers have begun to say a new thing about him: that the Gate Bearer is quiet, punctual, and does not complain. He has noticed that the Silver Leaf disciples no longer step aside for him in the corridors. They nod, and wait to see what he will do.

* * *

His mother's letters arrive every ten days.

They are carried up from the Garden by a Hill boy who has been taught to hand them to the steward and say nothing. This one is two sheets, in his mother's firm round hand, and he reads it standing at the window with the light going gray on the ice.

Jian,

We are well. The Hill families are settled. Wenjun has taught the nine without roots to read their own names, and Hu has taught the other five to hold a hammer. We are sixty-four. By the spring we will be seventy, if the beds hold. Your father says the number does not matter. I say it does, because I have to feed them.

Yue has decided to go. She says that she wants to see the library. I think she also wants to see whether you have changed. She does not say it, but she has been asking after your cloak.

The inspector has not come back. The Court's roll has been signed. The tribute is paid.

There is one thing more. I will put it plainly, because I do not know how else. A letter came, without a seal, in a clerk's hand, asking who was in the room the night you were born.

I did not answer. I have not answered. I want to know what to say.

Do not worry about us. We have lived through harder. But I would like to know whether I am right to be afraid.

Your mother.

He reads it three times. Then he sits down at the low table with a blank sheet and a brush, and for a long while does not write.

Who was in the room. He remembers nothing of that night, because it was not his to remember. A cradle, a coil, a bright cold light. A woman's hands. Whatever happened between the lab and the cradle belongs to the machine and the machine will not tell him. But someone knows the question to ask. Someone has read an old record and found a gap in it, and is pressing a finger to the place.

They do not know, he thinks. They want her to tell them.

He dips the brush.

Mother. Do not answer. Say nothing to anyone. Not to Father, not to Aunt Wenjun. If a second letter comes, bring it to me or to Elder Ye. It is not the question that is dangerous. It is the answer.

I will tell you everything I can when I can. Not by letter.

You are right to be afraid. You are also right to be careful. You have been both for twenty-eight years, and it has kept us alive.

Tell Yue yes. Tell her the library is large, and there will be a desk in the herbal room, and I will find her a good lamp.

He folds it, seals it with a thumbprint of wax, and hands it to the boy at the door. The boy takes it with both hands and runs.

That is the first thing he does on the forty-first day. The summons comes an hour later.

* * *

The envelope is plum-bark. He knows the paper before he touches it. He turns it over twice in his fingers, in the gray light of the corridor, with a cold feeling at the root of his neck. Then the steward who brought it clears his throat. "From Elder Ye, Silver Leaf. Not the Registry. She sent it by my hand. She said you would look at the paper."

Jian looks up. The steward's eyes are mild and tired and entirely innocent.

"She said you would look," the man repeats. "And that I should tell you the Sutra Hall uses plum-bark for all its notes. That it means nothing."

"Does it mean nothing?"

"I am only a steward," the man says apologetically, "but I have worked here for thirty years, and I would not say it means nothing."

The note is two lines. Tonight, after the third bell. The lower vault. Bring the book.

He holds it a moment longer. Then he folds it small, and puts it in his sleeve.

* * *

The lower vault of the Sutra Hall lies three flights below the ground.

He has been told he may not enter it without her, and so he waits at the top of the last stair in the lamplight, under a low arch of dark stone, until she comes. She comes alone. She carries a lantern, and a ring of keys on a cord, and her gray braid is pinned tight to her skull. She does not speak. She unlocks a door he had thought was a wall, and the air that rolls out of it is dry and cold and smells of old paper, camphor, and something older, like the inside of a temple bell.

"Close the door behind you," says Ye.

He does. The latch clicks. The lantern throws a small bright room out of the darkness, a vaulted cell with a table, two stools, and a chest of black iron bound in bands of dull brass. There are no windows. The walls are lined, floor to roof, with shelves of rolled scrolls, and each scroll wears a tag of ivory with a number in red.

"This is the Founders' Archive," Ye says. "There are eleven thousand items. The earliest are older than the Sect. I have read perhaps four thousand in forty years." She sets the lantern on the table. "Do you know what is in the chest?"

"No, Elder."

"Neither does anyone alive, Silver Leaf. I have a key. It was my teacher's key, and her teacher's before. It has never turned in the lock." She sits, and gestures for him to do the same. "Tonight, I think, it will."

She takes the ring from her neck and sets it on the table, and from it a small key of black iron, rough-cut and worn, the length of a finger. She turns it in her palm.

"Give me your hand," she says.

"Elder?"

"The Seal hand. The right."

He gives it. She does not take it. She holds the key an inch above his palm, and the iron stirs, very faintly, as a leaf stirs in a draft. The Seal beneath his breastbone answers with a low steady beat, and the key lifts from her fingers, rises into the air like a seed, and drifts across the table to the lock.

The chest opens with a long, soft exhalation.

Ye does not move. For a long moment she sits with her hands in her lap and her eyes fixed on the dark gap, and her face is that of a woman at the end of a long road who has come to a door she is not sure she wants to open.

"Forty years," she says. "I knew it. I did not think I would be alive."

* * *

Inside the chest, lined in gray silk, are three things.

The first is a book. It is thin and heavy, bound in black lacquered board, and on the cover in gold leaf, worn almost to nothing, is a single character: Roll. The second is a seal-stone, half of a round plaque of pale jade the size of a palm, with a ragged edge where the other half has been broken off, and a small hole through the center for a cord. The third is a folded square of cloth. It is white, plain, and very old.

"The Founders' Roll," says Ye softly, lifting the book. "The register of the Founder's disciples, in the Founder's own hand. The copy in the Sutra Hall upstairs is a transcript. It was made three hundred years ago, from this, by a scholar who was afraid of the original." She opens the cover. "The transcript lists six names. The Roll lists seven."

She turns it toward him.

The page is a heavy, creamy stuff, slightly yellowed. The ink is black and perfect. Seven lines, each written in a different hand, a column of names that run down the left side in careful rows: Yun Wuyi's six disciples, all of them known to the Sect's histories. The first six are in a firm clerk's script, large and plain. The seventh is different. It has been scratched out. Not torn, as Ye said. Scratched, with a knife, until the page beneath it has almost worn through. Only a few marks remain, in the lower corner of the line.

"The page was never torn out," Ye says. "I was wrong. It was only the name that was erased. By the Founder, I think, or at his order. The transcript was made from a copy where the line had been cut." She touches the scratched place. "I have wanted to know what stood here for forty years."

He leans closer. The marks in the lower corner are not in the Sect's characters. They are small and angular, set in a neat row. They are, he understands, with a lurch of the stomach that he does not allow to reach his face, the writing of the panels. The writing of the Dock.

I can read this.

The thought is perfectly clear. He sits still. The lantern ticks.

"You see something," says Ye.

"The marks are not in our script."

"No." She leans in, watching him. "They are not. I have taken them to every scholar of old scripts in the three provinces, under other names, with other pretexts. Not one could read them. Some said a southern cipher. One said a child's scratches." She lifts her eyes. "You looked at them for three breaths longer than a man who sees a cipher."

"I—"

"I do not ask whether you can read them." Her voice is dry and controlled. "I will ask you to say what they say. Aloud. Here, in the vault, with me as witness. I have a recording crystal in my sleeve that the Sect gave me forty years ago, and I will set it on the table, and you will read, and I will have the words."

He sits very still.

* * *

It is the cost, he sees, laid out as plainly as a bill.

If he reads the marks, the Sutra Hall holds a recording of Lin Jian speaking an unlisted language, in the Founder's own vault, to the one Elder who has waited forty years to hear it. She will not use it against him. He is nearly certain of that. But a crystal can be copied. A scribe can be bribed. A clerk with a perfectly trained hand can walk into the right office at the right hour, and a recording of the Gate Bearer speaking the Dock's tongue will be in a Registry drawer by dawn. It will be proof. It will be the one thing the polite, invisible people have been waiting for.

And if he does not read it, he loses her. He knows it as certainly as he knows his own name. Ye has risked her chair, her library, and forty years of patience on a single turn of a key. Refusing her now would not make her angry. It would make her sorry. She would put the crystal back in her sleeve and close the chest and walk him up the stair, and he would never be allowed in the lower vault again.

The seal-stone lies on the silk between them. It is humming. Not in the air, but in his chest, a deep slow pull, as a magnet pulls a needle. The Seal answers it in a rhythm like a second pulse.

Two of three, he thinks. The Dock told me. There are three fragments of the Gate-Seal, and this is the second.

He has to have it. He cannot walk away from it.

"If I read it," he says slowly, "I want something in exchange."

"I thought you might." Ye does not look offended. "Name it."

"The seal-stone. For as long as the review lasts. In my keeping, not the Sutra Hall's."

"It is the Hall's property."

"It is the Gate's." He keeps his voice level. "It pulls at my Seal like a hook. I do not think it will sit in a chest for two years without something happening. I would rather it happen where I am."

Ye is silent for the space of ten breaths.

"The Arbiter would have my chair," she says at last.

"Only if he finds out."

"You have a talent for impudence." She presses her lips together. It is not a smile, but it is the nearest thing he has seen on her face. "Very well. The stone goes with you. The cloth stays here. And the crystal runs, and I keep the words."

"The words only. Not my voice."

"You would have the crystal record in script?"

"I would have it record what I say, after I have said it, in your hand. Your own writing, in your own ink. Not a crystal." He meets her eyes. "A crystal can be copied by anyone who finds it. A page in your hand can only be copied by someone who has been in this room."

She considers. He watches her weigh it, a long thin pause with the lantern hissing between them.

"That," says Elder Ye, "is a better arrangement than the one I had." She takes the brush from her sleeve. "Read."

* * *

He reads.

The marks are only a line and a half. He has seen the script on a hundred panels, in the glow of a hundred menus, and he has never once spoken it aloud. It does not come easily. It sits in his throat like a stone. He begins in a low voice, and the first word comes out cracked, and the second smooth.

"Seventh Keeper," he says. "Record holder. Name withheld at own request."

Ye's brush moves. It does not stop.

"Duty: to keep the record of the Gate, and to see that none who is not named enter it." He swallows. "Left the Roll in year seven. Went out of the Sect. Took the book."

The brush pauses. She has gone quite white. "Took the book?"

"That is what it says." He reads the last line. It is in a smaller hand, as though added later, as though written by someone in great haste. He reads it twice before he understands it, and speaks it slowly.

"The Keeper's house will wear no name, so that no name can be taken from it."

The silence in the vault is perfect.

Ye does not write. She sits with the brush above the page, a drop of black ink gathering on its tip and falling, silently, onto the silk. Her eyes are fixed on the scratched line. Her face is very still.

"The ones who wear no names," she says.

It is not a question. It is a thing she is saying to the stone.

"You know the phrase?"

"My teacher said it." Her voice is a thread. "Forty years ago. On the night she disappeared. I thought it was a riddle. She said, beware the ones who wear no names, and I thought she meant the Blood Shadows." The ink drops again. "She was Core, Silver Leaf. A Core disciple. She was the finest scholar in the Sect. She was in this room the night before she vanished, and I have thought for forty years that she came here to read something. I believe now she came to read this."

He says nothing. He does not trust himself to.

"The Registry," Ye whispers. "It was founded six hundred years ago, by a Keeper of the Roll. By the seventh disciple. And it has been..." Her hand has begun to shake. "It has been keeping the record of the Gate since the day the Founders died. Waiting. It was never a clerk's office. It was a house."

* * *

They sit for a long time in the lantern's light.

At some point Ye gets up, and puts the book back in the chest, and the folded cloth beside it. She does not touch the seal-stone. She leaves it where it lies, on the silk, beside his hand. When she turns round her face has regained its composure, though not its color.

"Take it," she says.

He picks it up. The jade is smooth, cold, a half-moon with a ragged edge. The moment his fingers close on it the Seal gives a single deep, clean, golden beat, and a thin line of warmth runs up his arm and across his chest. For the first time in six weeks, the ache behind his breastbone goes quiet. He feels, for a heartbeat, whole.

"It likes you," Ye observes.

"It is the Seal."

"I will not ask." She lays the cloth in the chest and shuts the lid. The latch falls. "You have given me what I wanted. I will give you what I can." She pauses. "I will not lie to you, Lin Jian. The Registry is in this building. It is in every building. My own clerks are Registry clerks. I do not know which. I have trained half of them. The man who copied your note could be the boy who fetches my tea."

"Then what do we do?"

"We do nothing. Nothing they can see." She draws a long breath. "But the Roll is not the only record. Somewhere, there is a ledger of the Keepers' house. Names. Years. Who they have taken, and what they have done. If I could read it, I would know the shape of the thing we face."

"And you think it is somewhere I can reach."

"I think," says Ye, "that the Founder's seventh disciple took a book when he left. It is not in this vault. It is not in the Sect. But the last fragment of your Seal is the key to wherever it lies. I would stake my chair on it." She meets his eyes. "I know what I am asking. I am asking a boy of twenty-one to walk toward the one thing that has been hunting him since before he was born."

"You are asking me to find the third fragment."

"I am asking you to decide whether you will."

* * *

He climbs out of the vault at the fifth bell, with the stone against his chest.

It is the black hour, before dawn. The Sutra Hall's upper floor is dark and silent, the lamps in the stairwell burned down to red dots. He does not hurry. He walks the long corridor with Pebble on his shoulder and the jade humming under his tunic, past the closed doors of the scholars, down the stair, out into a blue cold that bites his lungs.

In the Inner Court's yard a small group is waiting.

Lin Feng stands at the front, in the silver-edged gray of a Silver Leaf, with his arms folded and his breath smoking. Beside him is a girl with a black braid and a satchel too large for her shoulders, whose chin is inked and whose eyes are wide and bright and just a little afraid. Behind them a steward holds a lantern.

"Brother," Feng says. "Yue has something to tell you."

The girl steps forward. She is shaking, a little, from the cold or from the dark. She clutches the satchel to her chest.

"I decided," says Lin Yue. Her voice is small and clear. "Mother Qinghe said I could say no. I thought about it for three days. I want to see the library." She swallows. "I told them yes. I am going to the Sutra Hall school. Feng will come on the days he can, and Elder Ye has said I can have a desk in the herbal room."

Jian looks at her. At the small determined face, the ink on her chin. At his brother's rigid, protective stance.

"You are sure?"

"I am sure." She hesitates. "I am afraid. But I want to see all the plants in the world. Is that wrong?"

"No," says Jian. His throat tightens. "No, Yue. That is not wrong."

"Will you teach me the Dock?"

He freezes. "The—"

"The strange writing," says Yue, with a child's bluntness. "Feng told me you can read the old marks. In the hall they say you can speak to the stones. I would like to know it. I would like to know all of it."

Above them, over the roof of the bell tower, the first thread of gray has appeared in the east. The stone in his tunic hums against his heart. The wind rises, and with it the faint smell of plum-bark and ink.

He thinks of the Seventh Keeper. Of the house with no name. Of a woman who has waited forty years and a boy who has not waited at all. He thinks of a third fragment, somewhere in the world, and of a ledger that holds the names of everyone the Registry has ever taken. He thinks that the bill for what he has learned tonight will arrive within the month, and that he has just agreed to pay it.

Every advantage has a cost, he thinks. And I have just bought three.

"Yue," he says at last. "I will teach you what I can, when you are older. For now, you will read the herbals and draw them as well as you do, and I will think about the rest."

She nods, solemn.

"And you," he says to Feng, quietly. "Come to my cell this evening. Bring Father's letters. I have a decision to make, and I need to say it aloud to someone who will not argue."

Feng's jaw eases a fraction. He puts a hand on his brother's shoulder.

"I will bring the wine," he says. "You can pretend to drink it."
